A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching v1 Appendices D–F to v2 Appendices F–H.

before.justification: Sections 7.1–7.2 report original computational protein-design experiments on the PDZ benchmark and molecule encapsulation, with quantitative results in Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds secondary-structure measurements, projected-diffusion comparisons and hyperparameter sensitivity results in Tables 4–7.

M1.justification: The predict-prox-renoise procedure, feasibility potential, ADMM decomposition and task-specific implementations remain unchanged. Correcting covalent to non-covalent terminology clarifies the existing hydrogen-bond geometry; it does not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 31 PDZ targets and box-and-cone molecule-encapsulation task. v2 explicitly retains the six newly identified poorly posed targets. Its sensitivity experiments use 6UBH, already within the benchmark, rather than introducing another dataset or task.

E2.justification: The original comparators remain, but v2 substantially expands the molecule-encapsulation comparison: Table 2 adds Recenter + CGD, and Appendix D evaluates Projected Diffusion Models with global-only and local-plus-global constraints. These introduce a combined-guidance control and a directly relevant alternative projection strategy.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark settings are retained. New evaluations introduce a secondary-structure percentage measured on relaxed structures using PyRosetta, plus controlled tests of lambda schedules 10/t, 100/t, 1000/t and infinity and one, two or three ADMM iterations on 6UBH. These are additional protocols, not demonstrated revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v1 lacks the dedicated sensitivity studies introduced in v2 Appendix E. Tables 6–7 test how constraint strength and ADMM iteration count affect feasibility, structural realism and diversity. Appendix D additionally documents boundary accumulation and nonconvergence under intermediate projection, substantially extending the analysis of design choices and failure modes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added tables continue reporting point estimates without introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Existing entries in Tables 1–2 and the runtime results are retained, but substantial new results appear. Recenter + CGD achieves 27.4% constraint satisfaction and 24.2% usable samples; both projected-diffusion variants yield zero usable samples. New analyses report 85.0% secondary structure for the proposed method and usable rates of 80.0%, 70.0% and 40.7% for one, two and three ADMM iterations. Section 7.2 replaces v1's table-inconsistent 53.7%/52.6% prose with the new combined-baseline results and revises the relative advantage from 4.8 times to approximately four times.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, assumptions, Theorems 6.1–6.3, ADMM derivation and proofs are substantively unchanged. The derivation and proof appendices move from E/F to G/H, with formatting and cross-reference edits.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about stochastic proximal sampling, ADMM decomposition, feasibility guarantees, the PDZ benchmark and state-of-the-art constrained generation. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 corrects the main PDZ description to non-covalent hydrogen-bond interactions and explains the complementary contacts supplied by the concatenated domain. It adds qualifications about short or geometrically restrictive ligands and interpretations linking excessive constraint enforcement or ADMM iterations to poorer fold preservation. However, Section 7.1 classifies 6UBH as poorly posed while Appendix E calls it well posed. Appendix A's general limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement says that code, the benchmark and reproduction instructions are released in supplementary material; their availability cannot be verified from these PDFs alone. v2 also documents the PyRosetta secondary-structure assessment and sensitivity settings. Existing hardware and implementation disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 8 adds Genie 2 and OriginFlow, citing Lin et al. (2024) and Yan et al. (2025), and discusses their limitations regarding global constraints. Appendix D expands discussion of the already cited Projected Diffusion Models. The broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: the PDZ task description is rewritten, bonding terminology is corrected, ethics and reproducibility statements are added, and two appendix sections are inserted. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 also adds the ICLR 2026 publication header.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the quantitative displays with new tables for secondary structure, projected-diffusion comparisons and two sensitivity studies (Tables 4–7). Table 2 gains a combined-baseline column, while the existing runtime table is resized and relocated as Table 8. Figures 1–4 retain their content.

improvement.justification: The combined-guidance control, direct projected-diffusion comparison and sensitivity studies strengthen support for the sampling design. Corrections to the main PDZ description and Table 2 narrative also improve accuracy. These gains are limited by single-target sensitivity testing without explicit sample-count or uncertainty reporting and the new contradiction over whether 6UBH is well posed.
